meta.title: The Canterbury Tales: The Full Story Explained (Geoffrey Chaucer)

scenes.narration: Thirty strangers at an inn agree to tell stories on the road to Canterbury — and those stories became the first great masterpiece of English literature.

on_screen.question: Thirty strangers, one road, a storytelling contest

scenes.notes: Hook before any title. ~26 words, minimal pauses. Names the work.

scenes.narration: The Canterbury Tales, by Geoffrey Chaucer, written around the year fourteen hundred.

Three things worth knowing before we set out. First: The Canterbury Tales is, in a very real sense, where English literature begins. When Chaucer was writing, in the late fourteenth century, serious books were written in Latin or in French; English was the rough, everyday tongue of the common people, not thought fit for great poetry at all. Chaucer's enormous gamble — and his lasting achievement — was to write a masterpiece in English, in the ordinary London speech of his own day, and in doing so he more or less proved, once and for all, that English could carry anything: tragedy, comedy, philosophy, filth, and prayer. That is why he has been called, ever since, the father of English poetry. Second: the Tales are built on one wonderfully simple idea. A group of pilgrims, travelling together from London to the shrine of the murdered Saint Thomas Becket at Canterbury Cathedral, agree to pass the long journey by each telling stories, in a kind of competition. That single frame lets Chaucer do something genuinely astonishing for his time — he gathers almost every rank and type of medieval society into one company on one road, from a noble knight down to a drunken miller, and then lets them speak, argue, boast, insult one another, and, above all, tell tales that reveal exactly who they really are. The storytellers matter as much as the stories. And third: the great surprise, for anyone expecting something dusty, pious, and solemn, is just how vividly alive the whole thing is. The Canterbury Tales are by turns noble, tender, savagely funny, and outrageously rude. There are high romances and earnest sermons, yes — but also drinking, adultery, swindling, and some of the best crude jokes in the language. It is a whole breathing human world, six hundred years old and still startlingly, recognisably modern. One more thing to know going in: Chaucer never finished it. He died with only a fraction of his vast plan complete. But even unfinished, what survives is one of the richest, funniest, most humane things ever written in our language. A quick word on Chaucer himself, because it helps. He was no cloistered scholar: he was a working Londoner, a civil servant and diplomat who spent his life among exactly the merchants, officials, soldiers, and churchmen he writes about, travelled to Italy and read Dante and Boccaccio, and knew the royal court and the customs house and the tavern alike. That is why the Tales feel reported rather than invented — Chaucer had met these people. In this retelling we can only follow a handful of the pilgrims down the road, so we will take the four most famous and most telling: the noble Knight, the drunken Miller, the roaring Wife of Bath, and the corrupt Pardoner. Together they show the astonishing range of the whole — from the highest romance to the lowest farce, from a meditation on fate to a horror story about greed.
scenes.notes: Context: birth of English literary tradition; the pilgrimage-frame gathers all of medieval society and the tellers matter as much as the tales; it is alive, funny, rude; unfinished.

scenes.narration: It begins in spring — with what may be the single most famous opening in all of English poetry. In April, Chaucer tells us, when the sweet showers have pierced the dry earth of March right to the root and coaxed the first flowers into bloom, when the soft west wind has breathed life into every wood and field, when the young sun is halfway through the sign of the Ram and the small birds sing all night long — then, he says, folk begin to long to go on pilgrimages. It is a gorgeous, rolling sentence that ties the religious journey to the oldest human stirrings of spring itself, the renewal of the earth and the restlessness it brings. And so the narrator — a version of Chaucer himself, who presents himself as a slightly naive, endlessly curious observer — finds himself one evening at the Tabard Inn in Southwark, just across the river from London, ready to ride to Canterbury. By chance, that same night, a whole company of other pilgrims arrives at the same inn, all bound for the same shrine: twenty-nine of them, of every sort and station. Before the evening is out he has fallen into fellowship with the lot of them and agreed to ride together. And then, before the story goes any further, he pauses to do the thing that makes the Prologue immortal: he describes each of these pilgrims, one by one, in a great gallery of portraits that together give us the whole of medieval England in miniature.
scenes.notes: The April opening (expanded); the narrator at the Tabard Inn, Southwark; 29 pilgrims arrive; he pauses to paint the General Prologue portraits.

scenes.narration: The opening lines — the birth of English poetry, in Chaucer's own spring-fresh voice.

on_screen.quote: When that Aprilis, with his showers swoot, / The drought of March hath pierced to the root…

scenes.narration: And what a company it is. There is the Knight, noble, modest, soft-spoken, and battle-worn, who has fought in holy wars across the known world and is, Chaucer says, the very flower of chivalry — a truly perfect, gentle knight. There is his son the Squire, a lovesick young dandy with curled hair and embroidered clothes, who can ride, joust, sing, and write poems, and is so in love he sleeps no more than a nightingale. There is the Prioress, a nun with exquisite table manners who speaks fashionable French, weeps over trapped mice, and feeds roast meat to her little lap-dogs — far more a genteel fine lady than a holy woman. There is the fat and jolly Monk who despises the dusty rules of his order and loves nothing on earth so much as hunting and a good fat roast swan; and the merry, charming, utterly corrupt Friar, who hears confession for a fee, knows every barmaid in town, and sells easy forgiveness to anyone who can pay. There is the threadbare Clerk of Oxford, a poor, thin scholar who spends every penny on books and learning, would rather own twenty volumes of philosophy than fine robes, and of whom Chaucer says the loveliest thing in the whole Prologue: that gladly would he learn, and gladly teach. There is the shrewd, red-faced, much-married Wife of Bath; the poor and genuinely holy Parson, who actually lives out the gospel he preaches and is the one true Christian of the lot; the huge, brawny, drunken Miller, who tells dirty stories and leads the company out of town blowing his bagpipes; and the two greatest rogues of all — the leering Summoner, and the Pardoner, who ride together making their living from the machinery of the Church itself. Chaucer paints every one of them with a sharp, affectionate, completely unillusioned eye, praising, mocking, and quietly exposing them, very often all in the same breath. And it is worth noticing how he does it: he almost never tells us outright that a character is corrupt, or vain, or holy. Instead he reports small, telling details — what they wear, what they eat, the little things they are proud of — and lets us draw the damning or admiring conclusion for ourselves. A monk's fur-trimmed sleeves and fat swan dinners, a friar's intimate knowledge of every barmaid in town, a knight's coarse tunic still stained with rust from his armour: each little detail quietly tells us everything we need to know. It is one of the first great exercises in the art of showing rather than telling, and it is a large part of why these thirty people feel so astonishingly, permanently alive. Then the Host of the Tabard — a big, loud, cheerful, bossy man named Harry Bailly — proposes a game to bind the journey together. Each pilgrim, he decrees, shall tell two tales on the way to Canterbury and two on the way home, and whoever tells the best of all shall win a free supper, paid for by the rest, when they return. He appoints himself judge, they all merrily agree, and in the morning they draw lots to see who shall begin. The lot falls, as if by fate, to the noblest of them all — the Knight.
scenes.notes: The portraits (expanded): Knight, Squire, Prioress, Monk, Friar, Clerk, Wife of Bath, Parson, Miller, Summoner, Pardoner; Host Harry Bailly's contest; the Knight draws first.

scenes.narration: Chaucer's verdict on the Knight — the whole chivalric ideal in a single line.

on_screen.quote: He was a very perfect gentle knight.

scenes.narration: The noblest pilgrim tells the noblest tale — two sworn brothers, one woman, and the blind cruelty of fate.

The Knight, fittingly, tells a grand, stately, philosophical romance set in the ancient world of Athens and Thebes. Two young knights, Palamon and Arcite, are cousins and the closest of sworn brothers, bound by an oath to stand by one another forever, through anything. But they are captured in war by Duke Theseus of Athens, and shut up together, for life, in a high tower — prisoners with no hope of ransom and no future but the four walls of their cell. And then, one fine May morning, everything changes. From their single barred window, high above the castle garden, they look down and see the Duke's beautiful young kinswoman, the princess Emily, walking among the flowers and gathering blossoms, singing to herself. Palamon sees her first and cries out as if struck; Arcite looks, and is lost in the same instant. Both of them, caged and condemned, fall utterly, hopelessly in love with the same woman at the same moment — a woman who does not know they are alive, and whom neither can ever hope to touch. And here is Chaucer's wry, serious point about the madness of love: in a single breath, that lifelong, sacred brotherhood curdles into bitter, jealous rivalry. They quarrel furiously through the bars of their shared cell, each insisting he loved her first, each claiming she must by rights be his, though both of them are locked in a tower and likely to die there. Love has made deadly enemies of the two dearest friends in the world, over a prize neither can possibly win. Arcite argues that love is a law unto itself, higher than any oath between men; Palamon, wounded to the heart, calls him a traitor and a false brother. Neither will yield an inch. And watching them rage at each other through the bars, we feel the full force of Chaucer's gentle irony: here are two noble, chivalrous, high-minded knights, the very models of courtesy — reduced in a single morning, by the sight of one woman at a window, to snarling like dogs over a bone that is not theirs and may never be.
scenes.notes: Knight's Tale: Palamon & Arcite, sworn brothers imprisoned by Theseus; both see Emily from the tower and fall in love; friendship curdles to rivalry.

scenes.narration: Then fate, which rules this whole tale, begins to twist the knife in earnest. Through the pleading of a powerful friend, Arcite is suddenly released from prison — but on one condition: he is banished from Athens forever, on pain of death, so that he can never set eyes on Emily again. Palamon, meanwhile, stays locked in the tower, but at least he can still glimpse her in the garden below. And so each bitterly envies the other: the free man who may never see her, and the prisoner who may. Years pass. Arcite, half-mad with longing, disguises himself and creeps back into Athens to take humble service in Emily's own household, risking death just to be near her. Palamon, after seven years, at last escapes from the tower. And by sheer chance the two meet again in a wood outside the city — and fall upon each other at once, fighting like wild animals, up to the ankles in each other's blood, over a woman who still has no idea either of them exists. It is Duke Theseus who stumbles upon them mid-combat. His first instinct is to have both put to death for breaking his laws — but, moved by the ladies of his court and by the sheer helpless extremity of their love, he devises something far grander instead. In one year's time, he decrees, each knight shall return to Athens with a hundred armed knights of his own, and they shall settle the matter in a great formal tournament, in a magnificent arena he will build for the purpose — and the winner shall have Emily's hand in marriage. The year passes; the arena rises; the day comes, blazing with banners and arms. And now Chaucer lets the gods themselves take sides, for each knight has prayed at a different altar. Palamon prayed to Venus, goddess of love, simply to win Emily. Arcite prayed to Mars, god of war, to win the battle. And both prayers are granted — cruelly, exactly, and to the letter. Arcite fights magnificently and wins the tournament outright. But as he rides in triumph before the crowd, the ground erupts, sent by the gods; his terrified horse throws him; and he is crushed and fatally injured in his very moment of victory. Dying slowly and nobly over the following days, Arcite forgives his cousin everything, and with his last breath commends Emily to Palamon as the worthiest man he knows. So Mars gave Arcite his victory, and Venus gave Palamon his love, and death claimed the winner — every prayer answered, every heart broken. After a long and solemn period of mourning, Palamon and Emily are at last married. And the tale closes on its hard-won philosophy, spoken by Theseus' aged father Egeus: that we are all of us pilgrims passing through a world we do not understand, ruled by a great chain of fate we cannot see the ends of — and that the only wisdom is to accept what cannot be changed, and to make a virtue of necessity.
scenes.notes: Arcite freed-but-banished, Palamon imprisoned then escapes; they fight; Theseus decrees a tournament for Emily's hand; Venus vs Mars — Arcite wins but is thrown and dies, gives Emily to Palamon; 'make a virtue of necessity'.

scenes.narration: Then a roaring-drunk miller shoves his way in with a tale that is the exact opposite of noble — in every possible way.

The company applauds the Knight's grand and solemn tale, and the Host, keen to keep things dignified, politely invites the Monk to follow with something equally lofty. But the Miller — huge, drunk, and swaying in his saddle — loudly insists on going next, and threatens to leave the company if he is refused. Chaucer, as narrator, mischievously apologises to the reader in advance and advises anyone of delicate sensibilities simply to turn the page. For what the Miller tells is a 'fabliau' — a short, bawdy, comic story of low life — and it is one of the funniest and filthiest things in all of English literature, told as a deliberate, cheeky, drunken slap at the noble romance that came just before it. Where the Knight gave us gods and honour and doomed courtly love, the Miller gives us lust, trickery, and a well-aimed insult. The story is this. In Oxford, an old carpenter named John has made the oldest mistake in the book: he has married a lively, pretty young wife named Alison, far too young and far too spirited for him, and he guards her jealously because he knows it. Lodging in their house is a clever, charming, and thoroughly unscrupulous young student named Nicholas, who studies astrology — and who very quickly sets about seducing Alison. She is more than willing; the two of them fall into a secret affair right under the old husband's nose, and spend all their cleverness plotting how to spend a whole night together without the carpenter knowing. There is also a complication, in the shape of a second admirer: Absolon, a dainty, fussy, over-perfumed parish clerk with golden curls, who is also mad for Alison, and who serenades her under her window by moonlight — to her very great annoyance, since she has eyes only for Nicholas. What makes the whole thing sparkle is the contrast Chaucer sets up so deliberately. The Knight's lovers were all sighs and prayers and noble suffering; the Miller's are all appetite and cunning and low animal energy. Where Palamon and Arcite gazed worshipfully at a princess they could never touch, Nicholas simply grabs Alison and talks her into bed within a page. It is love stripped of every courtly illusion, and told with enormous relish. And so, to clear the field and win himself an uninterrupted night with Alison, Nicholas hatches a scheme of wonderful, elaborate, ridiculous audacity — one that depends entirely on just how much the old carpenter loves his young wife and fears to lose her.
scenes.notes: Miller barges in with a bawdy fabliau mocking the Knight; narrator's mock-apology; old carpenter John, young wife Alison, student Nicholas (affair), fussy clerk Absolon; Nicholas's scheme.

scenes.narration: Nicholas persuades the gullible old carpenter, with much solemn nonsense about the stars, that he has foreseen a catastrophe: a second Great Flood is coming, even worse than Noah's, and it will drown the whole world in a single night. The terrified John begs to know how they might be saved — and Nicholas, straight-faced, instructs him to hang three large wooden tubs from the rafters of the barn, one for each of them, each stocked with food and an axe, so that when the waters rise in the dark they can cut themselves free and float safely away. He adds, gravely, that they must each wait alone and in total silence, and must not so much as speak to one another. The old fool, utterly convinced, does exactly as he is told, climbs into his hanging tub to keep watch — and, worn out, promptly falls fast asleep. The moment he is snoring, Nicholas and Alison climb quietly down and slip off to bed together, delighted with themselves. But the night has one more act. Absolon, the lovesick clerk, not knowing any of this, comes to Alison's low window in the dark and begs, as ever, for just one kiss. To be rid of him once and for all, she agrees — and in the pitch black sticks out of the window not her face but her bare backside, which the devoted Absolon kisses with great tenderness before he realises, with dawning horror, exactly what he has kissed. Humiliated and burning for revenge, he hurries to the village blacksmith, borrows a red-hot iron coulter, and returns to the window begging for one more kiss. This time it is Nicholas, feeling clever, who cheekily sticks his own rear out into the night — and Absolon brands him with the glowing iron. Nicholas, scalded, shrieks out 'Water! Water!' for the pain — and the old carpenter, jolted awake in his tub overhead and hearing that one word, is instantly certain the Flood has arrived. He grabs his axe, cuts the rope, and crashes down through the barn, tub and all, breaking his arm and knocking himself senseless. The whole neighbourhood comes running at the noise; and Nicholas and Alison cheerfully convince everyone that the poor old man has simply gone mad with fear of an imaginary flood. So the husband is left with a broken arm, a branded rival, and a reputation for lunacy, while the lovers get clean away. It is pure farce, built like a fine machine, every single thread — the fake flood, the hanging tubs, the window, the hot iron, the one shouted word — set up early and paid off together in a single glorious crash. And it is also, cleverly, a tale about the very sin the Knight's tale treated so nobly: desire. But where the Knight made love a matter of gods, honour, and tragic fate, the Miller makes it a matter of lust, cheek, and a scalded backside — and lets the self-important old husband, who tried to cage a young wife, reap exactly what such a man deserves. The company roars with laughter; only the Reeve, who was himself once a carpenter and takes the mockery personally, sits fuming, already planning the rude tale he will tell to get his own back. And that, in miniature, is how the whole book works: one tale provokes the next, the pilgrims needle and answer each other, and the road itself becomes a running argument about love, class, marriage, and morality, conducted entirely through stories.
scenes.notes: Nicholas's fake-flood scheme; three tubs in the barn; lovers slip away; the misdirected kiss in the dark; the red-hot iron brands Nicholas; 'Water!' and John crashes down; everyone thinks him mad; perfect farce.

scenes.narration: A woman married five times gives a roaring lecture on marriage — then tells a tale about what women really want.

The most unforgettable voice among all the pilgrims belongs, without question, to the Wife of Bath — a bold, worldly, richly dressed, gap-toothed cloth-maker who has been married five times, 'besides other company in her youth', and who delivers a long, roaring, brilliant prologue that is far more famous, and far more discussed, than the tale she goes on to tell. She has, in effect, hijacked the pilgrimage to argue her own case, and she argues it with tremendous gusto and a mountain of learning turned cheerfully to her own purposes. Why, she demands, should anyone be ashamed of marriage, or of marrying again, or of enjoying it? She has had five husbands at the church door and is ready, she says, for a sixth whenever this one dies. She describes, with gleeful frankness, exactly how she managed each of them: she bullied and out-talked and out-manoeuvred the three rich old ones, wearing them down until they signed everything over to her; and with the two younger husbands she learned harder lessons about love and jealousy and power, including a blazing marital brawl with her beloved fifth husband, Jankin, over a book of stories about wicked wives that he insisted on reading aloud to needle her — a fight that ended, tellingly, with her winning the mastery of the marriage after all. And that word, mastery — or 'sovereignty' — is the great theme of everything she says. What truly makes a marriage happy, she insists, from long and hard-won experience, is for the woman to hold the upper hand, to have governance of her husband and her own life. She says it all with such energy, such humour, such sheer overwhelming force of personality, that she steps straight off the page as one of the first fully alive, fully rounded women in all of English fiction — not a saint, not a symbol, but a real, loud, contradictory, unforgettable human being. And then, having thoroughly scandalised and delighted the whole company, she tells a short tale designed to prove her point exactly.
scenes.notes: The Wife of Bath's famous prologue (expanded): five husbands, defence of marriage & pleasure, how she mastered each, the fight with Jankin over the book of wicked wives, the theme of 'sovereignty'/mastery; one of the first fully alive women in English fiction.

scenes.narration: Her tale is set long ago, in the days of King Arthur. A young knight of the court, riding one day, comes upon a maiden alone — and rapes her. It is a shocking opening, and it is meant to be: the crime is real and the tale takes it seriously. For his offence the knight is condemned to death. But the queen and her ladies beg Arthur to let them judge him instead, and the king grants them his life to dispose of. The queen then sets the knight a strange sentence, and a chance: he has one year and one day to ride out into the world and discover the true answer to a single question — what is the thing that women most desire? — and if he returns with the right answer, his life is spared; if not, he dies. So the knight rides the length of the kingdom, desperately asking every woman he meets, and gets a different answer from each: riches, honour, fine clothes, flattery, pleasure, freedom, to be thought trustworthy. No two agree, and the year runs out. On the very last day, riding in despair toward the court and his death, he passes a forest and sees twenty-four ladies dancing — who vanish as he approaches, leaving behind only one foul, wrinkled old hag, the ugliest creature he has ever seen. She asks his trouble, and promises to give him the one true answer that will save his life — on condition that he grant her whatever she next asks of him. Out of pure desperation, he swears it. She whispers the answer in his ear; he rides to court; and before the queen and all her ladies he gives it — and it is judged, at once, completely right. What women most desire, he says, is sovereignty: mastery over their husbands, and governance of their own lives. Not one woman present can deny it, and his life is saved. But now the old hag steps forward to claim her promised price — and what she demands is that the knight marry her. He is appalled, revolted, bound hopelessly by his sworn word; and he weds her in black misery. On their wedding night, as he lies turned away in disgust, she gently challenges him, and then offers him a choice: she can remain old, ugly, and poor, but utterly loyal and true to him until she dies; or she can make herself young and beautiful, and take her chances with all the attention that beauty brings. The knight, who has learned something on his long year's journey, thinks — and then refuses to choose at all. He puts the decision in her hands; he grants her the sovereignty. And because he has finally given her the mastery she most desired, she rewards him completely: she becomes both beautiful and faithful, young and true, and they live out their days in perfect happiness. The Wife of Bath rests her case: give a woman the governance she wants, and husband and wife both win. It is a sly, clever, and surprisingly generous little fable — a story in which a man guilty of the worst kind of violence toward a woman is not simply punished but forced, slowly, to actually learn something: to stop seizing and start listening, to surrender control rather than grasp it, and to be rewarded only once he does. Coming from the mouth of a woman who has spent a lifetime fighting for the upper hand in marriage, it lands as both a wish and an argument — Chaucer giving his most vivid character the last word on the oldest battle of all.
scenes.notes: Wife of Bath's Tale: Arthurian knight commits rape, is set the question 'what do women most desire'; the loathly lady gives the answer ('sovereignty') for a promise; she claims marriage; the wedding-night choice; he yields the mastery and she becomes fair and true.

scenes.narration: A corrupt seller of fake relics tells the darkest, most perfect tale of all — three men who set out to murder Death.

The Pardoner is perhaps the most fascinating, and the most unsettling, of all the pilgrims. A pardoner's official job was to travel about selling the Church's 'pardons' — documents remitting the punishment for sin — and this one supplements his income with a bag of outrageous fake relics: a pillowcase he swears is the Virgin Mary's veil, a jar of pig's bones he passes off as the remains of saints. He is a smooth, cynical, theatrical con man who has grown rich on the credulity of simple country folk. And then he does something extraordinary. Warmed by drink and showing off to his fellow pilgrims, he openly confesses, before telling his tale, to the entire swindle. He explains, almost proudly, that he always preaches on one and the same theme — that greed is the root of all evil — and that he does so precisely in order to frighten poor, ignorant people into handing over their money to buy his worthless pardons and kiss his fake bones. He preaches against greed, he admits with a grin, out of sheer greed; he does not believe a word of his own sermons; he is a hypocrite to the bone, and he wants his clever audience to know it. His text, the Latin motto at the head of every sermon he gives, is 'Radix malorum est cupiditas' — the love of money is the root of all evil. There is something weirdly, bracingly modern about this. The Pardoner is not a secret villain found out by the story; he is a showman who has decided that honesty about his own dishonesty is simply the most entertaining card he can play, and he is probably right. And it raises a genuinely unsettling question that the tale will sharpen to a point: can a good and true story do its moral work even when it comes from a corrupt and lying mouth? Can the message be sound when the messenger is rotten? Chaucer leaves us to wonder. And then, having cheerfully unmasked himself as a fraud who grows fat on a lie, this thoroughly corrupt man opens his mouth and tells a tale so tight, so moral, and so genuinely terrifying that it rises far, far above the grubby soul delivering it.
scenes.notes: The Pardoner (expanded): sells pardons + fake relics; openly confesses his fraud before telling the tale; preaches 'greed is the root of all evil' out of greed; a self-aware hypocrite whose tale transcends him.

scenes.narration: It is set in a time of plague. Three young rioters — idle, drunk, blasphemous men — are carousing in a tavern early one morning when they hear a funeral bell toll outside, and learn that the corpse being carried past is that of an old drinking companion of theirs, taken in the night by a quiet thief called Death, who has been slaying people all over the countryside. Inflamed with drink and bravado, the three make a mad, solemn vow: they will become sworn brothers, they will hunt down this traitor Death wherever he hides, and they will slay him before nightfall and avenge every one of his victims. Off they stagger, drunk and furious, down the road to find Death and kill him. Before long they meet a strange, muffled, unbearably old man, who greets them courteously and tells them he longs to die but cannot, that even Death will not take him. They treat him roughly, and demand he tell them where Death can be found. Very well, says the old man quietly; if you are so eager to meet him, follow that crooked path to the great oak tree in the grove, for I left Death waiting there just now. The three race off to the tree — and find beneath it, not Death, but a huge, glittering heap of golden coins, more wealth than any of them has ever seen. In an instant, Death is utterly forgotten; the gold is all. They agree to guard the treasure until dark and then carry it home under cover of night, and they draw lots to decide who shall run into town to fetch bread and wine while the other two keep watch. The lot falls on the youngest, and he hurries off. And now the gold does its silent, patient work. The two who stay behind quietly agree to murder the youngest the moment he returns, and split his third between them. And the youngest, walking to town, decides exactly the same thing in reverse: he will keep all the gold himself. He buys poison from an apothecary, slips it into two of the three wine bottles, and starts back, smiling. He returns to the tree; the other two fall on him at once and stab him to death, just as they planned; and then, hot, triumphant, and thirsty, they sit down to celebrate their new fortune — and drink from the poisoned bottles, and die writhing in agony beside the man they have just killed. All three have found Death under the oak tree, exactly as the old man promised, and exactly as their own greed arranged. It is one of the most perfectly constructed short tales ever told in any language — a sermon turned into a flawless, chilling little horror story — and it is all the more disquieting for coming from the mouth of a man who has just told us, laughing, that he believes not one word of the moral it so brilliantly proves. And then Chaucer gives the episode a perfect, squirming finish. Carried away by his own performance, the Pardoner forgets that he has already confessed his fraud to these very people — and he launches straight into his usual sales patter, urging the pilgrims to come kiss his relics and buy his pardons for safety's sake, and even singles out the Host, Harry Bailly, as the most sinful and therefore the most in need, inviting him to pay up first. It is a staggering piece of nerve, and the Host explodes. He rounds on the Pardoner with a furious, obscene insult, swearing he would sooner carry the man's fake relics off and have them enshrined in pig's dung than kiss them. The Pardoner is struck speechless with rage, and for a moment the whole pilgrimage threatens to turn ugly — until the gentle Knight, the noblest of them all, steps in, makes the two men shake hands and kiss, and restores the peace so the journey can go on. It is the frame-story at its very best: the tales keep spilling back out onto the road, and the pilgrims remain as vivid, as prickly, and as human as anything they invent.
scenes.notes: Pardoner's Tale (expanded): three rioters vow to kill Death; the old man sends them to the oak; the gold; mutual betrayal — the two plot, the errand-boy poisons the wine; they stab him then drink the poison; all find Death through greed.

scenes.narration: Chaucer's full plan was staggering: over a hundred tales, two from each pilgrim going and two returning, with all the banter and quarrelling on the road in between. He completed only twenty-four before he died, and so the great storytelling contest is never actually finished, and the Host never names a winner. The pilgrims, on the page, never even arrive at Canterbury. And yet the unfinished fragment we have is a wonder, because of what Chaucer achieved inside it. In these tales he did something no English writer had done before: he gave us not stock types but living individuals — the drunk and bagpiping Miller, the loud and magnificent Wife of Bath, the smooth and self-damning Pardoner — and he gave each of them a story that fits them so exactly that the teller and the tale illuminate each other. The pilgrims interrupt, insult, and try to outdo one another, so that the frame itself, the road and the rivalry, becomes a human comedy every bit as rich as the stories told along it. Chaucer moved with complete freedom between the high and the low, the sacred and the filthy, the tragic and the hilarious, holding up a mirror to the whole of his society — knights and nuns, millers and merchants, con men and clerks — and finding it, by turns, noble, absurd, wicked, and endlessly, forgivably human. Why does it still matter, six hundred years on? Partly because it is the very root from which English literature grew — the living proof that our ordinary spoken language could carry the greatest poetry. But mostly because the people in it are still, unmistakably, us: vain, lustful, greedy, devout, kind, and above all desperate to tell and to hear a good story. Chaucer looked at humanity with clear, unsentimental eyes and enormous amused tenderness, and wrote it all down in the plain speech of the open road. Read him — in the original Middle English if you possibly can, aloud, for the sheer music of it — and you find yourself face to face with the first great voice in English, laughing at us, and with us, across six whole centuries. And that, in the end, may be the deepest reason the Tales have never died. Every one of these pilgrims is, like us, on a journey whose end they cannot see, passing the time as well as they can with the stories they have to tell. Chaucer understood that this is simply what human beings do — we travel together a little way, we talk, we boast and lie and confess and entertain one another, and the telling itself is how we bear the road. Six hundred years later we are still on it, and still telling. That is why, of everything written in the long history of English, this unfinished fragment remains one of the most generous and the most alive.

scenes.narration: That's The Canterbury Tales — a spring road, a company of strangers, and the first great chorus of voices in English literature, by turns noble, bawdy, savage, and wise. If you want more, there are full retellings of the other great books waiting on the channel, with more arriving all the time. Read Chaucer aloud, let the old words roll off your tongue, and listen to how astonishingly modern these six-hundred-year-old people still sound. Thanks for watching.
